kernelIdea: ¬(p ∧ q) is the same as ¬p ∨ ¬q, and ¬(p ∨ q) is the same as ¬p ∧ ¬q. Negation swaps and with or.

kernels.l1: Not both means one of them is missing. You do not know which one.
kernels.l2: When you cross out an AND telling, the AND turns into an OR. When you cross out an OR telling, the OR turns into an AND.
kernels.l3: The opposite of "both of these" is "at least one of them fails." The opposite of "at least one of these" is "both of them fail." Saying not to a joined statement swaps and with or.
kernels.l4: ¬(p ∧ q) ≡ ¬p ∨ ¬q and ¬(p ∨ q) ≡ ¬p ∧ ¬q. Pushing a negation inside a compound statement flips ∧ to ∨ and ∨ to ∧.
kernels.l5: De Morgan's laws say ¬(p ∧ q) ⇔ ¬p ∨ ¬q and ¬(p ∨ q) ⇔ ¬p ∧ ¬q; negation distributes across a connective only by swapping it.
kernels.l6: Negation does not pass through ∧ and ∨ unchanged — it swaps them: ¬(p ∧ q) ≡ ¬p ∨ ¬q and ¬(p ∨ q) ≡ ¬p ∧ ¬q. Assuming the wrong one is the standard error at the first line of an indirect proof.
kernels.l7: De Morgan's laws state that negation exchanges conjunction and disjunction: ¬(p ∧ q) ≡ ¬p ∨ ¬q and ¬(p ∨ q) ≡ ¬p ∧ ¬q. They are what let you negate a compound hypothesis correctly.
kernels.l8: De Morgan duality is the involution of the Boolean algebra that swaps meet and join; the same statement recurs for ∩/∪ on sets and for ∀/∃ on quantifiers.
